newsitem.title: USA: CBOT looks to add transparency to muni contract.
newsitem.headline: CBOT looks to add transparency to muni contract.

text.p: - The Chicago Board of Trade will propose an electronic system for displaying real-time dealer bid and asks for the 40 bonds in the municipal bond futures contract, an exchange official said Tuesday.

Steve Sural, director of the the CBOT's financial markets group, said the move would "add a little transparency" to the contract. He said the idea for the system grew out of a July meeting with members of an industry advisory council.
Kiki Melonides, an exchange spokeswoman, said she could not talk about whether the idea was related to a situation involving Susquehana Capital Corp. and the contract's June expiration.

Market participants had complained about diverse price movements between the index and the cash market during the expiration of the June contract. An executive at Susquehana has said the firm was hedging the risk of its long futures by buying bonds in the index.
Melonides also declined to talk about the status of the complaints with the exchange's surveillance department.

Sural said the cash market bid-ask system would need the cooperation of dealers, the Public Securities Association and vendors, who would be asked to disseminate the information to all of their users.
"We view it as something that will add value to vendor services," he added.

The CBOT is also proposing some fundamental changes to the index. One proposal would increase the minimum size of bond issues in the index to as high as $75 million to $100 million from the current minimum of $50 million, Sural said.

Another proposal would expand the evaluation time for determining whether to delete bonds from the index due to illiquidity to 20 to 30 days from the current 15 days. Sural said that change would give bond issues that tend to run hot and cold as far as cash market trading goes a better chance to remain in the index.
A third proposal would allow bonds that are deleted from the index to return as long as they continue to meet criteria for the index, he said.
"We want to make sure our index reflects the current, most-active bonds," Sural said.

He said all of the proposals grew out of the July meeting with the market advisory council. Members of the council will be sent information about the proposals "in the very near future," he said, adding that council members' reactions would determine whether the CBOT would pursue any or all of the proposed changes.
